description: Somos un equipo que quiere explicar las misiones espaciales con datos verificables. Nuestro proyecto, Atlas, muestra cada misión (Apolo, Artemis y otras) con su fuente, su fecha y su estado, para distinguir lo confirmado de lo programado. Yo soy Jhon Angelo: trabajo en tecnología e ingeniería de forma autodidacta, con experiencia en software y electrónica. Busco integrantes con diseño, redacción divulgativa o interés en datos de la NASA.
summary:
Astro fuente is an interactive platform that turns real space-mission history into something people can explore and learn from. Our original plan covered the full experience: an explorer of the solar system and the Milky Way; 3D views of real trajectories from missions such as Apollo 11 and Artemis II, showing distance, orbit and approach to the Moon; and a flight simulator where users build a rocket and attempt launch and landing. Every mission would cite its sources, and a feedback feature would let users report errors and suggest improvements. Future phases include Artemis III–V and an AI assistant that explains why each mission was designed the way it was.
The project was developed by a single person. The project was developed by a team of one person. Due to health problems, specifically a fever, we could only advance as far as the research and the project have reached, so this submission presents what we completed: a bilingual (Spanish/English) site with sourced mission data, where unverified figures are hidden rather than estimated, and a simplified vertical flight simulator whose physics is validated by automated tests against analytical solutions. We present it as a foundation to keep developing.
details:
What it does and how it works: Astro fuente is a web app built with HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript. A hash-based router renders the mission history, the sourced data cards and a flight simulator. The simulator integrates a simplified vertical launch with RK4 and Euler methods and checks the results against analytical reference solutions. The interface switches between Spanish and English.

Benefits and expected impact: Students and the public get a clear, sourced view of real missions such as Apollo 11 and Artemis II. Unverified figures are hidden instead of estimated, so users can see what is confirmed and what is still pending. The planned feedback feature would let users report errors, so the content improves over time.

Planned features (not yet completed): 3D trajectory views of real missions (distance, orbit and approach to the Moon), a solar-system and Milky Way explorer, multi-stage rocket simulation, and an AI assistant that explains why each mission was designed the way it was.

Tools: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML/CSS, SVG, the Node.js test runner, browser localStorage, and a SQL schema for the mission database, which is optional. Version control uses Git with conventional commits.

Creativity: The project turns a rocket launch into a playable simulator and pairs real mission data with interactive visuals. It also follows a strict rule: no figure appears without a source.

Factors the team considered: accuracy and transparency of sources, accessibility (bilingual interface, safe text rendering), physics validated by automated tests, and a scope realistic for a team of one person, which is why the project is presented as a foundation for future incubation.
